name: Chisel - SOCKS5 Tunnel
description: Chisel builds a SOCKS5 tunnel over HTTP through a firewall. Forward mode: run the server on the pivot and the client on the attack host. Reverse mode: run the server on the attack host (--reverse) and the client on the pivot with R:socks. Both expose a proxy on 127.0.0.1:1080.
source: CPTS Module 12: Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding

examples.label: OSCP Ch19 — serve chisel binary via Apache on Kali
examples.command:
sudo cp $(which chisel) /var/www/html/
sudo systemctl start apache2

examples.label: OSCP Ch19 — download chisel to victim and make executable
OSCP Ch19 — reverse server on Kali (port 8080, --reverse creates SOCKS on 127.0.0.1:1080)
OSCP Ch19 — reverse SOCKS client on pivot (R:socks = SOCKS5 listener on Kali 1080)
OSCP Ch19 — verify chisel SOCKS listener appeared on Kali
OSCP Ch19 — SSH through chisel SOCKS via ncat ProxyCommand

notes: Add 'socks5 127.0.0.1 1080' to /etc/proxychains.conf, then run tools with proxychains. Reverse mode helps when the pivot cannot accept inbound connections. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 19 (Tunneling Through Deep Packet Inspection). OSCP Ch19: chisel wraps traffic in HTTP to bypass DPI — key when SSH and raw TCP are filtered but HTTP/HTTPS outbound is allowed. Reverse mode (--reverse on server, R:socks on client): client connects OUT from the pivot to Kali, and Kali exposes a SOCKS5 proxy on 127.0.0.1:1080. No --socks5 flag needed on the server in reverse mode — R:socks on the client is sufficient. After tunnel is up, use ncat ProxyCommand to SSH directly to internal hosts through the SOCKS5 proxy without separate proxychains config.

references.title: HTB Academy - Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding
OffSec PEN-200 - Tunneling Through Deep Packet Inspection

recommended.note: Forces a tool's TCP traffic through a configured SOCKS/HTTP proxy (a pivot's SSH -D tunnel, an MSF socks_proxy, chisel, etc.).

steps.label: Download the chisel binary (attacker)
steps.command: wget https://github.com/jpillora/chisel/releases/download/v1.9.1/chisel_1.9.1_linux_amd64.gz && gunzip chisel_1.9.1_linux_amd64.gz && mv chisel_1.9.1_linux_amd64 chisel

steps.label: Copy chisel to the pivot host
Pivot: connect back as a reverse SOCKS client
Point proxychains at the SOCKS port
Route a tool through the tunnel

defense.why_it_works: chisel creates a fast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP(S) (client/server), commonly used to build a SOCKS proxy through a pivot where SSH isn't available.
defense.prerequisites: The chisel binary on both ends and an allowed outbound path (often 443) from the pivot.
defense.impact: A SOCKS proxy / port-forward over HTTP(S) into internal networks - works through web-only egress.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1090.001] A compromised host relaying traffic between segments it shouldn't bridge; an unexpected listening port (SOCKS/forwarder) on the pivot; the pivot initiating connections to hosts/ports it never normally contacts; lateral flows that appear to originate from the pivot (NetFlow/east-west monitoring).
defense.artifacts: The chisel process on the pivot; an HTTP(S) tunnel to the attacker; a SOCKS listener.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1090.001 M1030 Network Segmentation] strict east-west firewall rules so one foothold can't reach other segments; egress filtering; IDS/IPS + NetFlow analysis for proxy patterns and long-lived flows; alert on unexpected listeners on servers.
defense.evasion: Tunnel over an allowed protocol/port (443) and encrypt the channel so the relay blends with normal traffic; keep the listener on a common-looking port.
defense.misconfiguration: The network lacks proper segmentation — a compromised DMZ host has direct layer-3 reachability to internal infrastructure (database servers, DCs, internal admin panels). No egress filtering blocks outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections to arbitrary hosts, allowing C2 channels and reverse tunnels. Internal firewalls only filter inbound traffic, not east-west or outbound.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Network design: flat Layer-3 network, all VLANs can reach each other
# DMZ web server can ping/connect to: 10.10.10.0/24 (internal LAN), 10.10.20.0/24 (DB subnet)
# No egress proxy — direct outbound HTTP to any IP allowed

# iptables on pivot host (none blocking outbound):
iptables -L OUTPUT  # policy ACCEPT, no rules

# This allows: chisel client 10.10.10.5:8080 R:socks
# Attacker now has SOCKS5 access to the entire internal network
defense.secure_config:
# Network segmentation with explicit allow rules:
# DMZ -> Internet: only specific egress IPs (patch servers, DNS)
# DMZ -> Internal: ONLY the DB ports this specific app needs
# Internal -> Internal: segment by tier (web tier can't reach DC directly)

# Egress filtering — block all outbound except known-good:
# FortiGate / Palo Alto / iptables:
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 8.8.8.8 -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT  # DNS to specific server
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d <known_update_servers> -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# IDS/IPS signatures for Chisel, ngrok, frp traffic patterns
# DNS monitoring — detect DNS tunneling (dnscat2) via unusual query frequency/length
# HTTP proxy with TLS inspection — detect reverse tunnels in HTTPS streams
